subtopic: QUOTA ON SHIPMENTS OF LOBSTERS TO THE UNITED KINGDOM

speechtext:
Mr. J. V/aison MacNaughl (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries): Yesterday the hon. member for Queens (Mr. McLure) directed the following question to the department:
What is the quota to the United Kingdom on the shipment of lobsters for the year 1951? Is the quota based on cases or on dollar value?
Under the scheme of token shipments administered by the Department of Trade and Commerce, the 1951 quota for shipment of canned lobsters to the United Kingdom is fixed at forty per cent of the average annual value of exports of this commodity to the United Kingdom during the base period 1936, 1937 and 1938.
The 1951 quota amounts to $489,138.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during this tragic hour in the history of the world, when human rights are disregarded or flouted in so many different conflicts, it is pleasant to be living in a country such as ours. It is indeed pleasant to be living in Canada, this huge expanse where stout-hearted- people grow amidst security, because of an excellent administrative system that guarantees the highest degree of individual freedom as well as the full flowering of their activities, in their march towards progress, to which the unlimited resources of their country entitle them to aspire.
Canada is a great and beautiful land; it is truly a land privileged amongst all others, one towards which the economists say the eyes of the whole world are now turned.
I do not believe that I will mislead the hon. members of this house when I say that, in these modern times, Canada sets an example to the various countries of the world, as the stronghold of democratic liberties. Let us not forget that this remarkable fact, which goes unnoticed by none, never fails to stimulate the curiosity of foreigners, from the very moment they set foot upon our hospitable soil. We must admit, without fear of contradiction, that Canada is truly a privileged country and that, consequently, its citizens are entitled to consider themselves as particularly favoured by Providence.
It so happens that within this immense and extraordinary country which is this dearly beloved Canada of ours, there is a bit of land of which, as a member of this house, I am particularly fond. It has rightly claimed the better part of my being and thus fastened upon itself my constant and devoted attention. This constituency, Mr. Speaker, of which I am justly proud, to which I can promise my selfless support and sincere devotion, this constituency which is making such strides forward and shows such great promise of future greatness, whose present prosperity is beyond doubt and which is so remarkable from every point of view, this constituency whose picturesque vistas and truly great resources make it so attractive to tourists, this constituency which belongs to a province which was one of the earliest to join confederation and which borders, for the most part, on our majestic St. Lawrence is the constituency of Beauharnois which I am introducing to you today with feelings of sincere admiration.
As I said a moment ago, the constituency is prosperous in spite of depression periods

The Budget-Mr. Cauchon and many trying days. Perseverance has been rewarded by success. When Sir Wilfrid Laurier paid us a visit during his 1911 election campaign, at which time he won us over by the charm of his silver tongue, the great statesman was able to see that our district was in full activity and well on the way to success in the various fields of industry and trade. While travelling through the fertile countryside and the pleasant towns of Beauharnois county, he did not fail to show his just appreciation for the excellent work done by the farmers and the townsmen. But how surprised would have been the great and illustrious Liberal leader of 1911 if he could have accompanied our present leader in his triumphant tour of the same constituency in. 1949. The enormous and very real progress achieved would have surely held the attention of the great Laurier.
For, from that day on, our fellow citizens have followed, practically without a break, the ascending road to success and prosperity, which, according to Virgil, can best be attained through unremitting toil. That is why, Mr. Speaker, I repeat that I am really proud of the county I represent today, thanks to the confidence placed in me by my fellow citizens.
The people of Beauharnois constituency are peaceful and hard-working, true to their ancestral traditions. They have inherited the strength and valour characteristic of our forefathers, discoverers and pioneers of noble and pure stock. In different parts of the constituency, especially in the towns of Salaberry de Valleyfield and Beauharnois as well as in Chateauguay and many rural centres, there are people of different nationalities, French-Canadians and Anglo-Canadians, living and working side by side the whole year round in the most complete harmony. That feeling of brotherhood, which ensures good understanding and harmony between the two races, is really to be admired.
It is a well-known fact that our various ethnic groups live in the greatest harmony, showing the unity of their views in their daily relations. This fact constitutes an excellent and most important factor of success which makes life more interesting and more heartening and greatly increases the performance of all in striving towards a common ideal of comfort and prosperity. That is an outstanding example which I deem it my duty to mention in the house since it is in harmony with the great virtue


of charity, the main basis of the democratic ideal, a virtue which is so useful and so necessary today especially, to strengthen us in the face of present dangers. The harmony existing among the people of our riding deserves public recognition and should be brought to the attention of the entire nation since it constitutes such a powerful means of protecting the population from class struggles and of consolidating at the same time the entire social structure by upholding peace and security.
That union and cohesion of our people has brought quite wonderful results in our riding. Whenever there is a good purpose to be served in the matter of social welfare, such concerted effort becomes conspicuous and makes for the success of the various campaigns. In each case, our citizens have realized where their responsibilities lay and they have been equal to the task.
In due course, the city people as well as the farmers have shown that they knew something about business and that they were alive to their duties as Canadians, by answering generously to the call of their country at a time when all our forces had to be directed towards a common goal. Thus, our people have greatly contributed to making every loan drive a success, conscious as they were of the importance of such contribution for the safeguarding of our most sacred rights.
During the last war, as In the war of 19141918, the constituency of Beauharnois made a fine effort. A great number of recruits enlisted in His Majesty's armed forces. Various plants, on the other hand, worked on the production of war equipment and munitions. The same spirit of co-operation prevailed amongst related organizations such as civilian defence. All in all, worth finds and asserts itself. This is true of citizens of our constituency, whenever a generous effort, a helpful hand is required for a good cause.
In the constituency of Beauharnois there is a power plant noted not only in the district but throughout the country. It is an asset provided by the St. Lawrence river, the development of which is in the blueprint stage. It will contribute to the fuller use of the water power of this great river.
Mr. Speaker, I cannot resist the impulse to congratulate the Minister of Transport for the magnificent statement he has made on several

occasions in connection with the St. Lawrence seaway project.
The competence of the Minister of Transport is well known, but at the risk of offending his modesty, I must say that the brilliant outline he has made on several occasions of the St. Lawrence seaway project has brought much comfort to all those who have our country's development at heart.
The people of Beauharnois, Salaberry de Valleyfield and of the whole constituency are deeply interested in the seaway project because of the advantages which everyone, in his own sphere, would derive from this undertaking. Everyone favours and takes a keen interest in the vast project related to the deepening of our mighty St. Lawrence river.
The Beauharnois plant supplies power to an unlimited number of factories of every description. Beauharnois county has made a fine name for itself and is justly proud of the success achieved by a few of its sons in literature, fine arts, science and even sports. In the field of science, one of our citizens has gained recognition not only in Canada but abroad.
As regards social relations, employers and employees work in a spirit of co-operation and mutual understanding. In this connection, the workers have shown themselves well disposed; they are also very efficiently organized and enjoy, in this respect, every privilege granted by the established statutes. On the other hand, industrial leaders have shown a fine spirit of initiative where their employees' welfare is at stake. Undoubtedly, some claims are necessary and, at times, disputes did arise, but no regrettable incident has ever occurred and relations between salaried workers and industrial leaders were renewed on a harmonious basis. I have no doubt that these industrialists would be the first to press for the necessary measures if ever the government required of them a united effort for the common good. I am sure that the industrialists of Valleyfield, of Beauharnois and of other parts of my constituency would be the first to meet the wishes of the government in this respect.
(Text):
Now, Mr. Speaker, I wish to draw the attention of the house to a social problem which I encountered very frequently during my four years as mayor of the city of Valleyfield, and also while acting as director and vice-president of the union of municipalities for the province of Quebec. Until a few months ago this social problem was urgent, but because of recent international events
The Budget-Mr. Cauchon it has become for the moment less pressing. This problem is of concern to one of every three workers in Canada.
I am referring to all Canadian workers over forty, whose plight can be appreciated by even a cursory examination of the advertisements in any of our daily newspapers. In recent years it has been in the field of labour that the most severe economic losses have been suffered. Loss in the field of employment is always an obstacle which hinders progress toward other objectives. Thus it is important to solve first the problem of employment if we are to lead the way to a progressive economy. Both nationally and internationally, unemployment is a waste of productive resources. Indeed, when a section of labour is inactive, both production and revenue are lower than if there were employment for all.
Since the 1930's everyone who has the welfare of the workers at heart must be deeply concerned about the ever-increasing tendency to discriminate against those over forty-five. Except in skilled occupations the older worker who does not retain his employment is faced with much greater difficulty in finding new employment. This was proved during the depression, when the numbers of unemployed older workers increased. The war demand for labour of necessity did away with much of this discrimination. It also showed that the prejudice was not based upon the fact that the older worker did not do his work satisfactorily. Nevertheless, once the war was over the older worker in North America was found in greater numbers among the unemployed.
Some employers would have us believe that these workers are the inevitable victims of the machine age and the modern accent on youth. The entrance of ex-service personnel into the labour market has sometimes been used to justify or excuse such discrimination, which is often practised against veterans in that age group. Post-war demands all over Canada for manufactured goods and building materials were such that all workers were needed and should have been employed.
A moment ago I stated that the problem is an urgent one. In order to prove my assertion as to its gravity, one has only to consult the statistics issued by the officials of the national employment service. Vocational guidance and employment counselling are absolutely essential. This is not a mere expression of personal opinion; it is the considered opinion of those of the international labour office whose business it is to study the
2100	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Cauchon reports on unemployment from all over the world.
On page 89 of the book entitled "Action Against Unemployment," issued by the international labour office in Geneva for the year 1950, we find the following:
The main need of workers who lose their employment, apart from an income for themselves and their families to live on, is for technical assistance in finding alternative employment or the training or retraining required for re-employment. In present-day employment conditions it is too much to hope that individual workers will be able accurately to diagnose their own position and prospects and find their way, unaided, into the most suitable alternative employment available. Many of them, in fact the great majority, need access to vocational guidance or counselling services capable of helping them into suitable employment. The provision of such assistance is therefore an essential part of employment market action against unemployment.
The importance of guidance and counselling services for the unemployed was further recognized during the early part of the war when, despite labour shortage, the unemployed were not being absorbed as rapidly as had been expected. The process of re-absorbing ex-service personnel and war workers into peacetime economic life also gave new impetus to the development of guidance and counselling facilities. Finally, post-war full employment campaigns have included emphasis on such facilities as an integral part of action to ensure manpower distribution and redistribution contributing to the smooth and efficient working of the economy.
In 1949, the international labour conference, aware of the importance of these trends not only for promoting individual work satisfaction, but also for improving employment market organization, adopted the vocational guidance recommendation. This recommendation urges the rapid development of vocational guidance and employment counselling services and suggests standards to accelerate the development of these services along sound lines.
Our government was even quicker to recognize the situation, and in 1947 set up a counselling service in the city of Toronto. So successful has it been that Dr. Louis I. Dublin, vice-president of the Metropolitan Life Insurance Company, in an article appearing in the January 6 issue of Collier's- a United States publication-pointed to it as a method of coping with this problem which the United States is also attempting to solve. I quote:
Canada has already demonstrated what can be done along this line. Several years ago it found that almost half the men registered with the Ontario region of the national employment service were over forty-five, and that industry rarely offered openings for this group. So it set up in Toronto a free experimental vocational guidance service for older people.
_ Not only does a successful businessman like Dr. Louis I. Dublin approve such an attempt at organization, but we find the following on page 8 of the same international labour office book:
Experience has proved conclusively that the systematic organization of the employment market is an essential condition for the permanent control of the problem of unemployment.


The subsistence of those over forty-five is too vital to risk continual subjection to the hazard of negotiation. Again, in the same book at page 110 we find:
As unemployment increases, employer specifications with respect to age are tightened, and the percentage of older workers among job seekers rises. In a very loose labour market, older workers become over-represented among job seekers, and employers with a much larger reserve to choose from become increasingly reluctant to hire them.
An editorial in the Montreal Gazette of February 12 expresses similar views. The writer concludes that:
Canada as a nation will itself show signs of aging if it fails to adapt itself to the new problems that its aging population is creating. There will be a great need to revise old ways of thinking about age, so that the lengthening years of its workers may also provide for a lengthening usefulness in industry and business.
Reasons given by employers for their deliberate adoption of this policy of discrimination can be briefly stated as follows: (1) the high cost of group insurance premiums for older workers; (2) the high cost of company pension plans for older workers; (3) the older workers' inability to master quickly new industrial techniques; (4) the high accident rate among these older employees; (5) their lower output.
The first objection can be answered in a few words. One has only to compare the premium charged per thousand for workers at the age of twenty-five with that charged at forty. In one case the difference is as small as $1.58 per thousand.	,
What can be done to meet the second objection as to the cost of a company-sponsored pension plan? If pensions are computed, as they are in many cases, only according to the number of years employers and employees have jointly contributed, this objection does not hold. It has been shown that the older worker, desperately anxious for employment, may be willing to relinquish his right to participate in a company's pension plan. Why should he be obliged to give up his right to a degree of security when he is forced to retire? We must find a solution. It has also been suggested that the contributions of those employed for only a short period be remitted. The idea that we can continue to advance our civilization by insisting upon giving less and less for more and more is a dangerous illusion.
Inquiries which I have made in my constituency of those in charge of personnel in various industries would indicate that the facts do not support the contention that older workers are not adaptable. Their contribution during the war years is surely convincing proof of this. Their past experience should be of value to the employers, whose counselling services

could direct the older workers to tasks within their capacity. They need not be asked to learn entirely new techniques. Surely it is in the interests of efficiency to make use of the older workers' skill and experience. It is absolutely wrong to think that old age always impairs man's faculties. The greatest contributions in the fields of philosophy and culture have come from the minds of older men.
Accident cases in which compensation was paid prove that the high accident rates are in the twenty to twenty-four age group. The older worker is by nature more cautious, more deliberate, and more accident-conscious. If productivity declines as employers imply it does after the age of forty, how can they explain the fact that earnings on a piecework basis reach their peak between the age of fifty and fifty-five? When workers are asked to assume additional responsibility in any office, it is generally given to those whose age and experience enables them to handle ever increasing duties. These older employees probably have very heavy family commitments; they are less bored by routine; they are less likely to change their jobs, and are certainly likely to keep their minds on their work. All this contributes to high productivity.
Canada, like the United States, has become, gradually but inevitably, a nation of older workers. At present-and this percentage will increase with the advancement in preventive medicine-thirty-three and one-third per cent of Canada's workers are over forty-five. How could a rearmament program be carried on without them?
The only direct purchasing power is that of goods and services which are offered. Our economy needs their purchasing power; the country needs their contribution to its exchequer. The burden of taxation cannot be borne only by part of the population.
The young workers must, ini their own interest, support a policy of employment for all. They are separated by only a few years from that same category. Can they feel secure in an employment market which denies its oldsters the right to work and the self-respect which employment secures? This is their right in a democratic society.
Employers must remember that one of the most elementary desires of every human being is the preservation of his dignity. Is it not better for society or for a nation to provide work for its older members than to dole out a monthly pittance which degrades the dignity of the human being?
Employment and government must co-operate to solve the problem in the interests both
The Budget-Mr. Cauchon of industry and workers. Men are born with equal rights to work and to economic independence. Any worker who has to worry about losing his job because he has reached forty-five cannot produce as much as one who feels his job is secure. Nor can he feel free to seek a better job. One of our ideals expressed in the Atlantic charter is "freedom from want." Is want less distressing and intolerable in middle age than in youth? The movement to secure the social welfare of the workers carries in itself great hope but not only for those who benefit directly by it. Failure to obtain work because of this prejudice against workers of forty-five gives communism an opportunity to spread its ideology.
The very existence of democracy depends upon the active co-operation of labour, both now and in the future. If the situation is such that the labourer over forty-five is denied employment, democracy will surely suffer.
It is fortunate that the voters do not share employers' reluctance to trust those over forty-five with the nation's business. Who could bear to think of depriving the country of the accumulated wisdom represented on the government side of the house? Dare we mention the Senate?
Unquestionably work brings health, financial independence and happiness to all. It is essential to the welfare of mankind.
Those who think that this social problem is of concern only to labour and industry are not facing reality. It is a most urgent one, the solution of which will restore to the labourer his reason for living and his joy in working.
This is the situation as I see it. The Department of Labour has done everything in its power to win the co-operation of industry in solving this problem. It produced a film called "Date of Birth" which was shown throughout Canada by the unemployment offices of the country. Unfortunately industry's response was disappointing, and the situation has not improved appreciably. However, I am glad to know that the effort was not entirely wasted. Mr. George K. Foster, vice-president of the Canadian Johns-Manville Company, Limited!, in an address to the Royal Canadian Institute in Toronto on January 29, is reported by the Montreal Star of that date as follows:
Modern management is not just cold industrial efficiency. Modem managers are equally concerned with industry's human relations, with the dignity of man and with the harmonious co-ordination of men and machines.
2102	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Cauchon
This view is expressed not only by the vicepresident of a big company such as Johns-Manville, but also by a man who represents the boards of trade and chambers of commerce of all Canada. Mr. F. G. Winspear, president of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, in an article appearing in the "Monetary Times Annual National Review, 1951" and entitled "A fine new national spirit necessary in Canada," makes this statement:
As we move further Into this period of deepening crisis, I believe that Canadian business is ready and alert to assume its leadership which the country has the right to expect of it.
Also:
I believe attention should be directed toward the emergence of a fine new national spirit, the sense of enlightened leadership on the part of the business men of Canada.
Though it may be argued that we may be facing a shortage of manpower or a period of employment for all, and that this matter does not at present require immediate action, I am not in agreement with this point of view. In support of my contention, let me refer you to a report that was presented by the division director of the Department of Labour, division of research and statistics, at a public hearing of the New York state joint legislative committee on:	"Problems of the aging,"
December 9, 1948. This is a conclusion reached after a thorough study of the situation, and I quote:
As a group, however, the older workers are set apart by employment obstacles which leave them vulnerable to economic changes and with inferior status in the labour market even in periods of high employment.
Delegates to a conference on the problems of the aging, under the chairmanship of Dr. Albert Abrams, agreed that:
There are no insuperable obstacles to employment of older persons once management, labour and government sit down together to do the job.
I would propose that the federal government set an example to industry by employing in the civil service qualified older workers. These positions are suitable, for they require qualities which such workers generally possess-patience, judgment and experience rather than great physical strength.
The ability to work without the chance to do so means nothing unless we provide the opportunities.
According to a pamphlet put out by the institute of labour and industrial relations in connection with the university of Illinois and entitled "Who is too old to work?" we find on page 19, the statement:
Much of the success in making job opportunities for older workers will depend upon research findings.


As reported on page 70 of Hansard, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) made a statement as to the establishment of a national advisory council to make a survey of the manpower resources of the country. Would it not be desirable to instruct this advisory council to study at the same time this problem of older workers, in order to save these workers from suffering in a similar situation after the present emergency is over?
Perhaps even better would be the appointment of a special committee of the house to investigate fully means of making and finding job opportunities for older workers.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish at this time to direct my remarks to the speech delivered the other evening, by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), to deal with certain aspects of his budget speech and taxation proposals, and to refer in particular to certain paragraphs in his statement wherein he informs parliament and the country that the allocations for certain construction projects under the Department of Agriculture, the Department of Public Works and the Department of Resources and Development are to be curtailed, as part of the government's economy program.
I listened last night with a good deal of interest to the speech delivered by the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. McCusker). May I compliment him at this time upon his able presentation of the immediate need for the construction of a dam across the South Saskatchewan river in order to obtain irrigation and power development.
One of the main questions in my view is whether the budget is truly anti-inflationary, in the sense that it will prevent a further serious increase in prices, and whether or not the taxation proposals covered by the budget protect the low income groups within our nation. Of course the budget has to cover expenditures for the defence program. It is true that 10 per cent of the production of the country at this time must be used in the defence effort. But while the defence program is a real cost and burden upon the masses of the Canadian people, one group or one section in our economy has already benefited immeasurably by the present state of affairs in the world and the incident in Korea. I refer to corporations, and the profits of corporations after the payment of all taxes.
Corporation profits after taxes in 1949 were $1,171 million. In 1950 they had increased by $231 million to a total of $1,402 million, after the payment of taxes. Corporation profits from 1949 to 1950, after taxes, went up by 19-7 per cent, whereas the incomes of salaried

persons and workers in Canada increased in the same period by only 6-4 per cent. In the same period net agricultural income decreased from $1,513 million in 1949 to $1,424 million in 1950, a decrease of 5-9 per cent.
So this is the situation we have in 1950 compared with 1949: Corporation net profits, after taxes, are up 19 per cent, while salaried workers and labourers had an increase in their wages of less than one-third of that amount, or about 6 per cent. Then, the net income for farmers in Canada decreased within that period by approximately 6 per cent.
I say it is certain from those figures that neither workers' wages nor farm prices have contributed in the main to the inflationary spiral. Inflationary prices have been brought about mainly by corporations, monopolies, and semi-monopolies making increases in prices which were wholly unwarranted, and the result of which has been an increase in net profits, after taxes, in 1950, as compared with 1949, of over 19 per cent.
We have the minister's proposal of a surcharge or a surtax of 20 per cent on corporation profits, resulting in most instances in an increase in corporation taxes of 7 * 6 per cent. Does it follow from that proposal that corporation net profits in 1951 are going to be less than corporation net profits in 1950? I do not think it follows at all. Without price controls the great corporations of Canada are free to set the prices for their products. It will not be hard for companies like Massey-Harris, for example, to add on to their retail selling prices of machinery sufficient to pay the 7-6 per cent increase in corporation taxes, and sufficient to increase their 1951 net profits, after taxes, to a point higher than 1950 profits.
I say that without price controls the 7-6 per cent increase in corporation taxes, taken alone, can result only in one thing, and that is higher prices' and further inflation. The other proposals of the Minister of Finance do not improve-indeed they do not maintain the present standard of living of the lowest income group in our country. In arguing the advantages of a sales tax the minister said: Oh well, persons in low income groups have to pay the increased tax on only 25 per cent of their expenditures, and persons in the middle income groups from *$3,000 to $7,000 will pay the increased sales tax on only a third of their expenditures. Then he admitted that the incidence of the sales tax will decrease after the $7,000 income bracket.
The present increase in the sales tax is a regressive tax. It means a redistribution 80709-135
The Budget-Mr. Argue of purchasing power by taking it away from the lowest income groups in the country. When the minister came to increasing the tax on incomes he did not bring in a progressive increase by varying the percentage. Instead of doing that he placed on a surtax.

speechtext:
He placed on a surcharge of 20 per cent all across the board which, in my opinion, in no way compensates those in the low income groups for the increase in the sales tax and in no way compensates for the inflationary increase in prices that has taken place over the last few years.
The end result of all the tax proposals advanced by the Minister of Finance will be a further relative increase in the burden on the low income group. The minister increased the income tax on single persons earning $1,500 or less and on married persons earning $3,000 or less. We in this group do not approve of that part of the increase in the income tax. It has been said already a number of times by ministers of the government that 10 per cent of the production of Canada must be used in our defence program.
Let us look at the contribution already made by the married person earning $2,500 quite apart from the new burdens being placed upon him by this budget. If one compares the cost of living in 1949 with the last figure which was available on March 1 he will see that the purchasing power of a person earning $2,500 has gone down $263. In other words the effective buying power of people in that income group has been decreased already by more than 10 per cent. I think a further increase in income taxes on that group at this time is entirely unwarranted. There has been a reduction in purchasing power of $263; the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) adds a further increase in the income tax for this year of $15 and for a full year of $30; and there is also the increase in the sales tax.
The low income groups in this country have no means by which they can pass on their income tax to someone else. By charging higher prices corporations can pass on all of the increase in the corporation tax. People in the low income groups, those on old age pensions, those with large families are the people that should be protected by this budget, but they are the people whom this budget has failed to protect. They are the people upon whom this budget forces an even lower standard of living.
There is nothing in this budget to encourage people to save. If a person bought a $1,000 bond in 1945 he finds today that his $1,000 is worth only $665. There is no

The Budget-Mr. Argue incentive in this budget for Canadians to save. As a result of this budget prices can only go higher. As a result of this budget a further penalty is placed on savings. To that extent this budget is certainly an inflationary budget.
Over the last number of years this government has brought in some excellent social security measures. While some of them did not go as far as we in this group would have liked to have them go, nevertheless this government sponsored and enacted many important social security measures. For example, on April 1, 1949, a couple of months before an election-that may or may not have had something to do with it-the government increased its share of old age pensions so that old age pensioners might be paid $40 per month. Two years after that date the government by its inflationary method of finance and its failure to impose price controls took back $3.43 per month from the old age pensioners. The purchasing power of that $40 is today only $36.57.
The late W. L. Mackenzie King took to himself and to his government, and rightly so, a great deal of credit for the family allowance legislation which came into effect on July 1, 1945. Those payments were intended to make a redistribution of purchasing power within Canada whereby those in the higher income brackets had some of their purchasing power transferred to those in the lower income brackets who had large families. I think the family allowance legislation was excellent, but the money that was paid to mothers in 1945 should have had some protection from this government. The government should not have allowed inflation to the extent that the $5 cheque is worth only $3.32 today, while the $8 cheque for older children is worth only $5.32 today.
For the last few years, and particularly last year, this government has allowed a redistribution of purchasing power by permitting a further lowering of the standard of living of those in the lower income groups. The weak in Canada, the old age pensioners, those who must depend to a considerable degree on the family allowance cheques, and persons on pensions of various kinds are in no position to protect themselves against inflation, are in no position to pass on the increased burdens of this budget. But the strong, those who are well organized in labour unions, are able to get increases in wages which to some extent may compensate them for the present inflationary prices. The great corporations of Canada which made more profit in 1950 than in 1949 are in position to load their increased corporation tax on the backs of the Canadian people. It

is time that this government brought down a budget which would stop inflationary prices and protect the living standards of the ordinary Canadian people.
I wish now to refer for a moment to the South Saskatchewan river project. In every election for almost twenty years the prospects of the building of this dam with its consequent irrigation and power developments have been held before the people of Saskatchewan by the Liberal party. As a matter of fact every political party has supported this development. In 1947 an article appeared in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix, which article was quoted on a previous occasion in this house by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker). This article read in part:
It will be two years before construction work can begin on the South Saskatchewan river dam.
That the South Saskatchewan project will be carried out, let no one doubt. Mr. Gardiner has committed the present government to the undertaking, according to a report of his speech at Lethbridge the other day.
It was to be two years from that date before construction could begin on that great project. That brings us to 1949. In the election campaign of that year the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) made many statements with relation to the advantages of the South Saskatchewan development project. He called upon the people of Saskatchewan to send to Ottawa an increased number of members of the Liberal party to sit with the government, and he said: By doing so you will ensure that the dam will be built. I should like to quote from the Regina Leader-Post of June 23, 1949, the report of a speech made by the minister at Lemberg. It reads as follows:
"The South Saskatchewan project would provide cheap power and encourage building of industries in small towns, provide an incentive for young people to stay in this province. I think we have made a fairly good start now," said Mr. Gardiner. "Send us back to complete the job . . ."
They sent the Minister of Agriculture back to complete the job, and within a few months after the election during the first session in the fall of 1949 the minister said: Well now, the completion of this project will depend upon the province of Saskatchewan paying large sums of money towards its final completion. He even said at one point that he might hold a gun at the head of the government of Saskatchewan to the point where he would ask them to pay 50 per cent of the cost. As I understand the situation, the Saskatchewan government has now agreed to pay the share the Minister of Agriculture has said would be equitable. But even though Saskatchewan has agreed, the Minister of Finance in his budget speech has

apparently scuttled any prospects for the building of this very necessary project. The Minister of Finance has this to say at page 1801 of Hansard:
We have paid particular regard to our expenditures on construction . . . Examination of the estimates for the Department of . . . Agriculture reveals very large reductions in their construction programs, notwithstanding urgent needs for expenditure of this kind, following twenty years during which works have been postponed, first for lack of funds, then for war, and finally, in recent years because of shortages of materials and labour.
There never was any lack of funds. In the depression days the government should have found the money, as it well could have, to build this project. The people of Saskatchewan did not complain when it was postponed during the war, but we have never admitted that there was such a severe shortage of materials and labour following the war that a start on the project could not have been made. Now we have the defence program taking, as the Minister of Finance says, only 10 per cent of the production of Canada, and the Minister of Finance has apparently squelched any chance there was of getting the South Saskatchewan development project started and finally completed.
I want to say to the Minister of Agriculture that, even though we in the west feel that he failed to obtain a satisfactory settlement from the government with respect to the five-year wheat pool, we do not want him to fail to obtain this very necessary project. I say to the Minister of Agriculture that if he cannot secure approval for the project from the government he should dissociate himself from the government and leave it. The project is so important to the welfare and rehabilitation of the province of Saskatchewan that at this stage the Minister of Agriculture should dissociate himself from his colleagues in the cabinet if he fails to have the project approved.

The estimates that might be used for this project have been decreased from a total of $2,770,000 to $2,045,000.
