speechtext:
I think we should view the project, Mr. Speaker, in the light of its actual cost to the government with relation to our defence program. I support the defence program. Nevertheless I believe that it is possible to construct the dam without in any way detracting from our defence program. In the-estimates this year for the Department of National Defence our defence expenditures amount to $1,600 million. The total cost of this project is $68 million for the federal^ government, not to be spent all in one year' but spread over ten years, or a cost to the federal government of less than $7 million a year, a cost of less than one-half of one per cent of our present defence program. If the government wished, certainly it would be possible to proceed with the construction of the project at this time.
I have always believed that the building of more tanks, guns, planes and ships is only one aspect of our defence program. Coupled with that there should be economic aid to the underdeveloped countries. According to this morning's press, 40 million people in India face starvation. As our share in the Colombo plan the government has earmarked $25 million. The government of India turned down the suggestion that part of the $25 million should be spent on the purchase of feed wheat from Canada. I do not blame India for thinking she might spend the $25 million to her advantage in some other way. But I say that the government should offer 100 million bushels of wheat as a gift to India, and other

The Budget-Mr. Fleming backward nations in need of food, without any strings attached and apart altogether from the Colombo plan.
If we are to protect democracy in the world, and if we are to spread democracy to other nations, one of the things we must do, and soon, is provide food to the starving peoples of the world. We must help the backward and underdeveloped countries. If the government would go ahead with the irrigation project on the South Saskatchewan river we could greatly increase our production of foodstuffs. I believe $7 million a year spent on the construction of that project would be as valuable to Canada by way of providing for defence as any $7 million of the $1,600 million in the estimates for national defence. If we are to protect democracy we must see that the underdeveloped countries have technical assistance and that the starving peoples of the world are adequately fed. If we do that we can help protect ourselves against the inroads of communism; and as a part of our defence effort I suggest that the government immediately [DOT]embark upon the development of the South ."Saskatchewan river.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the remarks I propose to offer this afternoon will relate directly to the budget, both the proposals submitted by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and the speech which accompanied them. The bare, hard facts of this budget are these, in a word. This year the government is proposing to take out of the pockets of the people $3,730 million; to spend $3,700 million, and at the end of the year have a surplus of $30 million. Of that total contemplated expenditure of $3,730 million we are told that defence will cost $1,664 million and the non-defence expenditures and supplementary estimates will account for the balance of $2,036 million.
The minister reported that in the year just closed he extracted from the pockets of the people $3,105 million; that he expended $2,902 million, and had a budgetary surplus of $203 million. In order to achieve his goal this year and take from the people $3,730 million he proposes now to apply new taxes and increased taxes which will yield revenues not of $3,730 million per year but of $3,900 million. Just two years ago, on the eve of the election of 1949, the minister was at great pains to see that the estimates then introduced should not amount to a sum as large as $2,000 million. Therefore the estimates for that year were conveniently put just a fraction below that figure, at $1,985 million, so that with characteristic windowdressing on the eve of the election the government might say it was not going to take

an amount as large as $2,000 million out of the pockets of the people. Now this same minister expresses the fear of budgets of $4,000 million a year. What a change!
Let us measure the objectives of the Minister of Finance as disclosed in his budget speech. What has he sought to accomplish in the budget he has introduced? Well, we know what he is seeking to raise by way of revenue, and we have heard what he proposes to spend. What are the objectives he holds before parliament and the people in asking support for these estimates of revenue and expenditure? He has announced his objectives in these terms: "the pursuit of peace and the control of inflation." Let us then measure the proposals in the light of those announced or professed objectives.
As far as the pursuit of peace is concerned, I am sure there will be no haggling in this house about any necessary expenditures on national defence, as long as this house can be sure the taxpayers of the country will receive value for the money so spent. We will have to acknowledge that as the machinery of parliament is now constituted there is little effective opportunity for a parliamentary check on these vast expenditures on national defence; and, far from assisting parliament in devising new and improved procedures for checking these expenditures, the government has taken a sort of gleeful pleasure in defeating any constructive proposals put forward to that end. Apparently they do not want any assistance from parliament in surveying the expenditures they propose.
Then let us look at the other announced objective of the Minister of Finance, the [DOT]control of inflation. Would that this budget might accomplish this end! Would that it could make some effective contribution toward combating the forces of inflation! It is evident that the government is not sufficiently aware of what those forces of inflation are doing to the budget of the average Canadian family. If you want a good measure of the extent of inflation, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that you turn to page 6 of the white paper tabled by the Minister of Finance, where you will find the figures on the gross national product taken first at market prices and then in terms of constant dollars on the 1935-39 basis. This will show that a good deal of the so-called "buoyant revenues" and a good deal of the so-called prosperity of the country have been simply a fiction of figures and a measure of the elasticity of the Canadian dollar.
In 1939 the gross national product, measured in those two ways, was almost equal in value. At market prices it was

$5,598 million and in constant dollars it was $5,523 million. Then we come forward to 1946. In that year the gross national product at market prices was $12,008 million, while in constant dollars it was only $8,902 million. In 1949 the gross national product at market prices was $16,382 million, while in terms of the constant dollar it was only $9,648 million. On the preliminary 1950 figures we are told that the gross national product at market prices was $18,000 million in round figures, but in constant dollars only $9,982 million, or barely more than half. That is the gross national product to which the government is wont to refer in glowing terms when trying to picture the present situation.
The minister has said he wants to balance his budget. I do not think a single member of this house will have any disagreement with that professed objective. We all wish to see this budget balanced this year; but we do not wish to see the minister building up big surpluses at a time when the cost of living is pressing with an ever-increasing, intolerable weight upon the average Canadian family. There was a time when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) talked in the terms that are used by those who believe in the theory of the managed economy, and when, under the same guidance, he apparently believed it was his function to siphon off purchasing power by budgeting for a surplus. We saw that in the way in which he resisted the legitimate demands for decreases in personal taxation. In presenting this budget he has not used the jargon of those who believe in the managed economy, but one can sense the presence of that theory pervading the speech.
Now, that leads me to make an observation on budget surpluses and accurate budgeting. I submit, sir, that the first duty of a minister of finance in submitting a budget is to give the house a true estimate, and as accurate an estimate as can possibly be devised, of the expected revenues accruing from the various fields of taxation. There must be no covering up. We will not expect any superhuman ingenuity in estimating revenue, but we will expect that there will be no attempt at covering up, either of fact or of theory. I am not suggesting that there has been any deliberate covering up here of a budgetary surplus- in the figures the minister has put before us, but I do say that the best that can be said for the figures put before us in this budget, having regard to the record of these past five years, is that this budget, like its predecessors, contains the vice of inaccurate budgeting. In presenting this budget the Minister of Finance has been guilty, as in the past, of a chronic underestimation of revenues.
The Budget-Mr. Fleming With possibly one exception, sir, that has had a very misleading effect upon all budget debates in the last five years.
Inaccurate budgeting, sir, not only has a misleading effect on the house in leading the house into the approval of rates of taxation which are not justified to meet the legitimate expenses of government, but it also has a very harmful effect upon those who are charged with the management of the nation's finances. With budgetary surpluses rolling up during the year the inevitable effect upon the minister and his colleagues in the government, who are so often looking for opportunities of spending more money, is to create a loose attitude on their part towards expenditures. We have seen many examples of it.
When we are talking about budgetary surpluses, let us come down to the hard facts, and acknowledge that these budgetary surpluses do not reflect any credit on the Minister of Finance. They simply establish the fact that he has taken more money out of the pockets of the people, in most cases hard-earned money, than has been required to meet the legitimate expenses of government. If you want evidence, sir, of the loose budgeting that has occurred during recent years, let me give you some figures. These figures I am giving now are for the fiscal years ending on March 31, of the year I shall mention. In 1947, the minister budgeted for a deficit of $260 million. At the end of the year he turned up with a surplus of $374 million. He was just out $634 million in his calculations. In 1948 he budgeted for a surplus of $350 million. He turned up at the end of the year with a surplus of $676 million. In other words, he was out $326 million in his calculations. In 1949 he budgeted for a surplus of $549 million. He turned up with an actual surplus at the end of the year of $595 million. That year he was out $46 million. Then 1950, that is the fiscal year ending March 31, 1950, reflects the largess of this government on the eve of election. According to the previous pattern of budgetary surpluses the Minister of Finance budgeted for $202 million, which at the end of the year proved to be $131 million. He was out $71 million that year. You will notice that in that year the error is in the other direction, for this time he underestimated. Those of us who recall the way in which the government, during the election campaign in 1949, used public money to create good will for the government to serve its partisan purposes, will not have to look very far for an explanation of the budgeting error revealed in those figures.
In this year just closed on March 31, 1951, the Minister of Finance, even after he had an opportunity last September to revise his

The Budget-Mr. Fleming budget estimates, announced an estimated surplus of $20 million. He turned up at the end of this year with a surplus of $203 million. Let me remind you, sir, that was after having provided $65 million of expenditure of an extraordinary nature recently that was no part of the original budget. He finishes up with a budget surplus of $203 million, and this $65 million is not the only expenditure of an extraordinary nature which the Minister of Finance incurred in the closing days of the fiscal year when he saw that he had this comfortable surplus.
If you will total those figures, sir, you will find that in round figures for the last five years the minister has been out something like $1,200 million in his estimates. The net average is about $240 million a year. If the Minister of Finance is running true to form this year, and there is no reason to think he is not, the budget surplus for which he now budgets, namely, $30 million, may be expected to turn out to be something like $270 million. On those figures, sir, there is no excuse whatever for any increase in the sales tax; there is no excuse for any of these increases in commodity taxes. There is very little, if any, justification for any increase in taxation at all.
What has the minister achieved by way of economies in expenditures, because he used some brave words about the necessity on the part of the government for reducing expenditures on non-defence items? Out of a total contemplated expenditure during this fiscal year of $3,700 million, the minister asks the house to regard as a great achievement on his part the fact that non-defence items have been reduced by $35 million as compared with last year. Poor little thing-$35 million! It is less than one per cent of the amount he is proposing to spend this year. That is the achievement of the Minister of Finance in carrying out all his brave talk about the way in which he was going to economize this year and reduce expenditures. Remember, if you will, that the reduction of $35 million on non-defence items was based on a comparison not with a year of slight expenditure but with a year of swollen expenditure, because in the fiscal year ended March 31, 1950, this country spent more than in any year since 1946.
We will not soon forget the brave words used by the Minister of Finance in this house last September 7, 1950, when at page 420 of Hansard he said:
I can assure the house that this search for economies will be pressed forward, and that in preparing the estimates for next year a rigorous standard of essentiality will be applied.
I Mr. Fleming.]

The result of those efforts is a reduction of less than one per cent in the total expenditure. What an accomplishment! What a triumph of labour on the part of the Minister of Finance! What ground for a due return of thanks to his colleagues that he offered in the course of his budget speech last Tuesday night!
Now, sir, when we are talking about economies and the elimination of extravagance in this budget, when we call for the squeezing of the water out of this budget of expenditures, we of the opposition say: Which would you rather have? Would you rather have some contraction of these expenditures, or do you prefer an increase in taxes, an increase in the sales tax, an increase in commodity taxes, an increase in the personal income tax? Well, the answer of the government is that apart from this trifling and inconsequential reduction of less than one per cent as compared with the total expenditure this year, they apparently prefer to soak the people of Canada with these new and greatly increased and oppressive exactions.
Where is the economy drive that the Minister of Finance so bravely talks about? Sir, it is abundantly clear that this government is impotent to undertake any serious drive directed at the elimination of extravagance. It is no credit to this government that when members of the opposition have been critical of the government because of extravagance and wastefulness, and when we have put forward concrete proposals for the establishment of machinery here that will give the house an opportunity of participating in this design of the economy drive, the government, as I said earlier, has taken gleeful satisfaction on every occasion in defeating those efforts. Here we are, still lumbering along in this house with this clumsy old procedure of committee of supply, with every member of the house a member of the committee. We still have the clumsy, awkward procedure that never gives any member of the house an opportunity of getting down to details of this problem in a way that would be possible if we had some up-to-date procedure in the form of a special committee of the house on the estimates. But the Minister of Finance will not have a committee of the house sitting on the estimates to give detailed scrutiny to those estimates. So far as the poor old standing committee on public accounts is concerned, it is not given an opportunity to do anything with respect to the estimates. It is to be compelled to be content with reviewing stale expenditures. So, sir, let us be perfectly frank. There is in the present machinery established by this

house no effective review of proposed expenditures. We might as well admit the fact, and the government, with its tyrannical use of its majority in this house, simply defeats our efforts to apply that effective scrutiny which those swollen expenditures demand.
Is there any extravagance? Well, sir, time alone prevents my giving in greater detail some of these examples of extravagance; but let me remind you of just one or two examples. Last year, my colleague, the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton), put before the house the startling-yes, shocking- fact that expenditures on travelling, publicity and sundries in the estimates of that year totalled $49 million, exhibiting a startling increase year by year, as the government spending machine has demanded more and more oil. What do we find this year has been accomplished by the government in this so-called "economy drive" in relation to travelling expenses? Well, we find, sir, that the Minister of Finance reports an increase in the appropriation for travelling and removal expenses, going up from $27,786,602 in the year 1950-51 to a figure of $36,309,109 for this current fiscal year. Let me remind you, sir, that the figures last year included defence expenditures as well. If you take out the defence expenditures in both years you will still find that the contemplated expenditures this year by the government on travelling show an increase as compared with last year.
Is it not about time, Mr. Speaker, that some effective brake was applied to many of these expenditures, which cannot be justified in times like these when the government is making these huge impositions on the people? And yet, where there is this deliberate choice between soaking the people on the one hand, and effecting necessary reductions in extravagant expenditures on the other hand, this government's deliberate choice is the soaking of the people with more and more taxes.
Let me turn now to some of these proposals of increases in the already heavy load of taxation borne by the people of Canada, and let us especially measure these proposals in the light of the professed object of controlling inflation. Here we see an increase of 20 per cent in the personal income tax, and the Minister of Finance thinks that he is entitled to great credit for not having reduced the exemption below the present relatively low figures of $1,000 for single persons and $2,000 for married persons without dependents.
Let me remind you, sir, that when these exemptions were established two years ago the Progressive Conservative party in this house, and on the hustings in the election
The Budget-Mr. Fleming campaign that followed, demanded exemptions at that time of $1,200 for single persons and $2,400 for married persons. Measure today the burden of the increase in the cost of living on people of low means, and I think you have there a sufficient refutation of the claim of the Minister of Finance for any credit whatsoever for not having reduced these already very low exemptions.
Then he goes on to impose sweeping increases in indirect taxes. He proposes to take $3,730 million out of the pockets of the people this year as compared with what one might have thought was quite a heavy load of $3,105 million last year. Thus this year in the 11J months which remain between now and the end of the fiscal year on March 31, 1952, the Minister of Finance proposes to take $625 million more out of the pockets of the people than the swollen sums that he took last year. Let us examine these indirect taxes, because the Minister of Finance has announced sweeping increases in the sales tax from 8 per cent to 10 per cent, and a sweeping increase as well in other commodity taxes in the form of excise taxes.
We say, sir, concerning these indirect taxes which are levied at the producer's level, that they are all subject to certain inherent vices. There has been no effort on the part of the Minister of Finance to grapple with these vices in announcing sweeping increases in taxes of that nature. He is going to go on taking more than 40 per cent of his total revenue this year in the form of these indirect taxes.
In the first place, sir, they are hidden. The people do not have an opportunity of measuring the extent of the taxes that they are paying when they buy things which have already been subjected to these heavy indirect taxes.
In the second place, these taxes pyramid as they pass from hand to hand. Several years ago I gave in the house an actual example of a manufacturer who sells his product at $1 a unit. He adds the 8 per cent sales tax. He sells to the wholesaler. The wholesaler adds his 20 per cent mark-up, not only on the $1, but on the 8 cents tax as well. It passes on to the retailer, who in turn adds a 50 per cent mark-up, not only on the tax, not only on the mark-up on the tax, but on the 50 per cent mark-up on the mark-up on the tax.
Consequently, in that case what the consumer pays is not 8 per cent, but 14-4 per cent. And if by chance there should be one other hand in the process through which those goods pass, for instance a jobber, the

The Budget-Mr. Fleming poor consumer will pay, not simply as in the case I gave, a mark-up on the mark-up on the tax, but he will be faced with a mark-up on the tax, plus a mark-up on the mark-up on the tax, plus a mark-up on the mark-up on the mark-up on the tax.
What does the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) say about all that? He not only accepts the process, but he wants to go on and increase the tax. In that way, by an increase in the tax at the source, you will find that the spread, the pyramiding, will increase greatly. It will be far more than in the case I gave, from 8 per cent to 14-4. In that case the increase will spread by the additional 25 per cent to 18 per cent.
That brings me to an observation concerning taxes of this kind, that the government gains less than the consumer pays on account of the tax. The government does not receive in that case 14-4 per cent. Under this shocking tax the minister will not be collecting 18 per cent. No, he will receive 10 per cent, as in the former case he received just 8 per cent. And what justification can there be for taxes of that nature, where the government gets into its coffers far less than the consumer has to pay on account of the imposition of the tax?
Those are weighty enough reasons in normal times, but in a time of inflation, surely this is far from being a time when taxes of this nature should be increased. It is a time when, if the government were really serious in trying to combat inflation, it would be reducing taxation of that kind. And I say to you that the sales tax in this budget ought to have been reduced, if the government really meant seriously to confront the problem of inflation with a series of effective measures.
The fourth vice of the hidden tax, which is so objectionable at a time like this, is that the government inevitably increases the cost of the goods, but it does not create any more goods in the process. It simply intensifies that process of inflation which has been described as too many dollars chasing too few goods. This kind of taxation does not create any more goods; it simply increases the cost of the goods.
Now, do you recall the year 1935, when the late Mr. Mackenzie King went up and down this country during the election campaign of that year and, as reported in various dispatches of the Canadian Press, denounced the sales tax in these words:
That iniquitous tax which presses alike on the rich and the poor.
"That iniquitous tax"-do you heed those words? And yet the Minister of Finance
I Mr. Fleming.]

today is proposing an increase in that iniquitous tax.
When the late Hon. J. L. Ralston as minister of finance, on June 24, 1940, came to make his budget speech, he dealt with the subject of the sales tax in these words:
We realize that increases in indirect taxes disguise the burdens imposed by the war but they are much more likely to distribute these burdens harshly and unfairly.
And what Mr. Ralston had then to say about the burden of war taxes can be applied with equal force and validity today to these increases in taxes necessitated by the expansion of our defence program, as well as by the government's inability to curb its own vaulting extravagance.
When Mr. Ilsley in the following year made his first budget speech, on April 29, 1941, he said this:
An increase in the sales tax has, I think, been fairly generally expected. At least, there are evidences of a good deal of buying in anticipation of such an increase. This tax, while comparatively easy of administration and collection and extremely productive, has marked defects as a fiscal instrument. After extended consideration, we decided on balance against any increase. In coming to this decision, we were not forgetful of the problems of agriculture, which would have been intensified had the sales tax been raised.
And, sir, by the increase in the sales tax today, following Mr. Ilsley's sound reasoning, the burden which agriculture is unfairly being called upon to bear today will thereby be intensified.
Then Mr. Ilsley had something further than that to say in peacetime, because when he brought in the budget on October 12, 1945, he had this to say concerning the sales tax:
I have been impressed also with the extent to which the sales tax is having a discouraging effect on the rapid and efficient modernization of our productive equipment.
And later on he says:
Particularly we should remove those taxes which, imposed far back in the production process, increase costs out of proportion to the contribution which they make to the revenue.
Mr. Speaker, could you have more effective indictments than those of the sales tax, in general, and thereby of the proposals the Minister of Finance has put before the house that those burdens should be intensified now, and that the iniquities of these indirect hidden taxes should! now be multiplied? The Minister of Finance should be called upon in this house to withdraw his proposal for this 25 per cent increase in the sales tax. At a time when people are having so much difficulty in purchasing clothing, boots, shoes, shirts, furniture, let us remind ourselves that these necessities of life are subject to the sales tax, and that that tax is going to be

greatly increased. The Minister of Finance could not have done worse than he has done in this proposal.
And, sir, his proposals with reference to commodity taxes are open to the same kind of objection. I wish I had time to review them; but what he has done, apparently, is to choose out many things that are necessities for most people, and to pass over such things as liquor, in the process. He has fastened on things like irons and ironers, electric kettles and electric toasters for an increase from 15 to 25 per cent in the tax which was unfairly imposed upon them last year.
He goes farther, and he applies that tax, now increased to 25 per cent, to a range of articles which were not subject to it before, including clocks and watches, fountain pens, luggage, shopping bags-with the exception of paper ones-and I suppose we will all be carrying paper shopping bags soon, under this budget. It includes cameras also. There has been no attempt in the budget to distinguish between articles that are expensive, and thus extravagant, and articles which are not expensive, and are necessities for people in every walk of life.
He comes along and imposes a new 15 per cent tax on electric stoves, hot plates, washing machines and refrigerators, thereby inevitably increasing inflation and casting further heavy impositions upon young married people.
While at the same time he makes a great to-do about reducing the tax on candy and soft drinks, let us look a little further and heed the effect of the sales tax. I read in a dispatch from Toronto, as reported in the Globe and Mail of April 13, that a board of education committee meeting was told by business administrator Fuller that the increase to 10 per cent from 8 per cent in the general sales tax would add $4,000 to the price tag on classroom supplies, such as scribblers and pencils.
Now, can you imagine anything more utterly foolish than to heap all these exactions on the things that people have to buy, and thus intensify the unfairness of a tax which bears more heavily, relatively, on people of small means?
And sir, in measuring the inflationary effect of the budget, and the futility of the policy of the government, let us not forget that there are already rumblings of demands for a general wage increase, as a direct result of these burdensome impositions.	.
There is another aspect of this matter to which I should like to refer. At the dominion-provincial conference the government came 80709-136
The Budget-Mr. Fleming forward and apparently agreed to an amendment to the constitution to give the provinces the right to levy a 3 per cent turnover tax. While that matter was under discussion, while negotiations were proceeding between the dominion and the provinces; after giving the provinces to understand that it would facilitate an amendment to the constitution to permit them to levy that objectionable kind of tax, this government now comes forward and slaps on a 2 per cent increase in the sales tax from 8 to 10 per cent. They beat the provinces to the gun, and have made it that much more difficult for the provinces, even in the unfortunate event that there should be an amendment to the constitution permitting them, to impose such a tax. This government has made it virtually impossible for the provinces, having regard to the actualities of the taxing situation, to use that taxing power, for that would mean an increase from 8 to 13 per cent in these taxes levied at the consumer level, or a total increase of 62-5 per cent in this kind of tax as a result of these measures of the government. In that way I say that the government has broken faith with the provinces.
There are just two more matters I should like to discuss. I wish to say just one word on the subject of personal savings. I am sure that there never was a time when it was more desirable that people should have the opportunity of setting aside personal savings. As under the inflationary heat they watch their savings in the form of life insurance melt away, they need more savings with which to buy more insurance in order to protect themselves and their families. At this very time the Minister of Finance reports that last year there was a drop of $270 million or 30 per cent in the total personal savings in Canada. That is a most significant decrease when you consider that the national income in terms of the same kind of dollars has been rising rapidly. The budget is going to take another $625 million from the personal savings of the people, which last year were just $645 million. Unless there is some relief for the people, unless the figures change, unless there is an increase in savings or some relief so that they may increase their personal savings, this budget is going to take all of last year's total personal savings in Canada, less $20 million.
I say in conclusion that if the purpose of this budget was to stimulate inflation, the minister could not have done a more effective job. On the other hand, if his purpose was, as he professes, to control inflation, he could not have done a much worse job. This budget and these taxes will intensify inflation. They will accelerate inflation. They abet inflation.
2112	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Shaw They share in inflation. This budget profits by inflation. This budget was conceived in inflation, and it proposes to live on the avails of inflation.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first remarks of this afternoon will relate specifically to the financial proposals contained in the minister's budget. After having completed that reference I intend to deal with the Canadian coal mining industry, which industry at the moment is suffering considerable stress and strain. After having listened to the speeches delivered yesterday by the three opposition leaders I am forced to conclude that there is actually little left to say with respect to the principal weaknesses in the budget unless I am to indulge in rather prolonged repetition.
Hon. members will appreciate that because of the arrangements for speaking in this house the financial critic of the official opposition is placed in the position of being able to move an amendment if he so desires. The second speaker is the leader of the C.C.F. who is in position to move a subamendment, which was done in this case. That leaves us in the position where we are not able to move an amendment even though we should desire to do so. Even when a decision has been rendered on the amendment and subamendment we are still prohibited under the rules from moving an amendment.
I should like to turn for a moment to the amendment moved by the financial critic of the Progressive Conservative party. This amendment asserts in its first paragraph:
The proposals of the Minister of Finance are unsatisfactory because they will inevitably increase the cost of living for all and especially for those least able to bear it.
My leader indicated in the course of his remarks yesterday that that is the conviction which we hold.	The second paragraph
asserts:
This house condemns in particular, as inflationary, the increase by 25 per cent of the general sales tax and is of the opinion that the increase is unnecessary and unwise.
In the course of his observations my leader indicated that we concur in those observations. The third paragraph reads:
This house further condemns the heavy increase in excise taxes on certain essential commodities and is of the opinion that much of the government's proposed huge increase in taxation is due to its own extravagance.
Before a decision is reached on this section I should like to have one or more Progressive Conservative speakers elaborate upon that reference to extravagance. I realize fully that it is an easy reference to make, but I


would feel much better if the subject could be elaborated upon by a subsequent speaker. The fourth clause reads:
The house regrets the failure of the government to take effective steps to deal with profiteering.
We concur fully in that. The leader of the C.C.F. (Mr. Coldwell) added a further clause to that amendment, reading as follows:
This house further regrets the failure of the government to exempt from the proposed 20 per cent defence surtax the incomes of single persons up to $1,500 and the incomes of married persons up to $3,000.
We concur in that. If the exemptions which prevailed prior to the very substantial increase in the cost of living were just, then it is particularly proper that we should press at this time for the raising of those exemptions. When 1 examine the budget I am personally convinced, be the facts what they may, that it was thrown together in a hurry. It reminds me very much of the housewife who is an afternoon bridge addict and who discovers about five minutes to six that her husband will be home from work almost immediately after six o'clock and it will be necessary for her to rush home, slap some things together and call the result a dinner. That is the impression I cannot help but take out of the budget.
The minister has asserted that his purposes are twofold: First, to raise money to meet government expenditures and, second, to use financial methods as an economic weapon designed to influence and control the factors working upon the economy. In simple language, it was an attempt to curb the inflationary trend.
Obviously the minister had in mind the killing of two birds with the one stone. The minister's almost savage bites at income, and let us not forget for one moment that he sank his teeth deeply into moderate incomes, is designed to siphon off enough purchasing power to reduce prices. I am personally convinced, as has been said by previous speakers, that the things which he has done must inevitably have a completely opposite effect to that which he seems to desire. The sales tax has been characterized as being iniquitous. Knowing the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) as I do, I rather fancy that if he had not been quoting when he used the word "iniquitous" he would have found some much more effective and appropriate language with which to describe it. If I were anywhere except here I believe I could think without any difficulty of appropriate language with which to describe the increase in the sales tax. The increase of 25 per cent will certainly aggravate the position of the low and middle income groups.

The excise tax on washing machines, stoves and refrigerators is like a twisting and grinding foot that has been on the throat of the ordinary man for all too long already.
After having increased the burden of costs on the low and average income groups by increasing the sales tax and by imposing an excise tax on additional commodities, the minister then deliberately hit below the belt by imposing an additional 20 per cent surcharge on income tax. I think that the Canadian consumers, particularly those in the low or middle income groups, can quite properly cry foul. However, since the minister is not only the offender but the referee the little fellow can only cry foul in vain. Actually the whole budget represents nothing more or less than a kick in the teeth of those who during the past several months particularly have laid such emphasis upon the rapidly increasing cost of living which, as has been stated by my leader more than once, is undermining the health of many Canadian people, is lowering their morale, and could in effect actually threaten Canada's defence effort.
Because of higher taxes, because of higher living costs-and they are certainly going to be higher as time goes on-it is inevitable that organized labour and others will demand higher wages. Let us make no mistake about it. The result is certainly bound to be a swamping of any good purposes which the government may have had in mind, or hoped to accomplish, as a consequence of the budget. Obviously the government and the Minister of Finance have found it desirable to either overlook or forget that fact. It was said by the Minister of Finance that the sales tax does not apply to so-called staple foods. It is argued that because of this it will not increase costs for a good many people. May I ask the minister this question? Even though for the sake of argument, we were to accept his view that it will not increase costs, can he say that it will decrease costs to the Canadian people? His answer could not be yes under any circumstances.
As I have stated once or twice already, it is going to increase the cost of living of the average family in Canada. While still referring to the sales tax, I might say that I received a communication from one of my constituents only today. It is not often I get a request that entails so much difficulty in the preparation of an answer. This chap submitted this to me and asked me to comment. I cannot comment so I am going to put it on the record and let the minister or the parliamentary assistant to the minister do so. He refers to the sales tax as part of
The Budget-Mr. Shaw a vicious circle or, as he calls it, part of the house which Abbott built. He says that first you have the sales tax. Then you have the rise in the cost of living to pay the sales tax. Then, he says, there is a demand for higher wages to meet the rise in the cost of living to pay the sales tax. Then, he says, there is the granting of the demand for higher wages to meet the rise in the cost of living to pay the sales tax. Then he says there will be an extra issue of money or more taxes to meet the granting of the demand for higher wages to meet the rise in the cost of living to pay the sales tax. Then he says there is likely to be devaluation of the extra issue of money to meet the granting of the demand for higher wages to meet the rise in the cost of living to pay the sales tax. Then he says there must be, according to his way of thinking, another sales tax to-or has Mr. Abbott's house by this time collapsed?
I hope that either the minister or his parliamentary assistant will indicate to me some time during this debate whether this man's thinking is right or wrong, and if it is fallacious I should like to know in what respect. Certain of these so-called non-staple goods include tea, coffee, cocoa, mustard, relishes, prepared household beverages, vinegar, flavouring extracts, sauces and so forth. The minister knows as well as all other hon. members of the house know that, while we cannot properly categorize these things as staples, they are found on almost every table at each and every meal. In effect they have become staples. They are to be taxed, and the tax is to be heavier as a consequence of the 25 per cent increase in the sales tax.
It was said in the house yesterday that certain merchants have taken advantage of these tax increases to extract from the Canadian people actually more than the new taxes represent. There is no denying that fact. I would be the first to admit that most merchants are perfectly honest. However, there is evidence that in some cases not only is the tax which has been imposed larger than that which the increase actually represents, but certain merchants impose the taxes on goods which they had in storage in large supply, and the government cannot possibly benefit as a result of the additional tax upon them. The Canadian consumer, however, is bound to suffer as a result of prices going up when it was not necessary for them to do so. Where definite evidence of that sort of thing can be found I think that action should be taken to impose penalties.
Since the minister delivered his budget statement, I have read a number of statements such as the following: It could have
80709-136J
2114	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Shaw been worse. Certainly it could have been worse, but in my opinion that is a poor standard by which to judge. It is very much like a doctor saying to an individual: Brace up, my friend, you have chicken pox; it could have been worse; it might have been smallpox. My opinion is, and has been right along, in spite of everything contained in the budget, and in fact because of certain things contained therein, that certain effective action must be taken by the government now to stop the ever-spiralling cost of living. We must remember that, at this very time when we are presumed to be developing a defence program within our nation, at a time when we are presumed to be developing security measures designed to combat sabotage within our country, at this very time when we are participating in external conflict outside of our country, at a time when we are supplying arms to those who, with us, desire to preserve the democratic concept of life, we are doing other things which can in effect destroy our entire effort to make the maximum contribution toward the preservation of democracy.
Yesterday the financial critic of the Progressive Conservative party quoted Stalin's reference to currency. I think there are numerous quotations which could be taken from communist propaganda and which would be just as effective. Karl Marx, who together with Engels produced the communist manifesto, stated more than one hundred years ago that there was only one way to kill capitalism; that was by taxes, taxes and more taxes. Had he been dealing with the situation today he might have said crazy taxes and crazier types of taxes, because that seems to be the trend in our country.
I appreciate that a substantial portion of the taxation now imposed results from obligations which arise in connection with the defence of our country. The other day I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) if it were the intention of the government to set up a defence expenditures committee, comparable to the war expenditures committee which served during the war and to the war expenditures and economies committee which functioned shortly after the war. In view of the fact that we intend to spend $5,000 million for defence purposes over the next three years I am convinced it is absolutely imperative that a committee of this kind be set up without delay. I am not favorably disposed toward referring this matter to the public accounts committee, but I will not elaborate on that point.
Yesterday the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) made reference to small loan companies. I had intended to 

refer to those companies myself, and had good reason for doing so. When certain credit restrictions were adopted, I understand voluntarily in part, the small loan companies across the country became as active as beehives. As a matter of fact I rather feel there may be some intrigue in high places. During the Easter recess two cases came to my attention, and without mentioning names I should like to indicate to the house the nature of those cases. One man wanted to expand his small business, and negotiated a loan from a chartered bank. He was advised that the money would be available, but before he had an opportunity to use it he was advised that "due to government regulations" they had to withdraw the loan. Within two days the manager or a representative of one of these small loan companies approached this man and said, "We hear you require $2,000. We are in a position to make the money available to you." Where did that man get his information? Only two men knew about this, the businessman and the bank manager. There may be some significance in the fact, as he said to me, that these small loan companies can compound their interest to the point where the borrower is paying 18 per cent. It could be that there is connivance between these financial institutions.
That is as far as I am going, except to say that recent statistics indicate that the loans made by small loan companies have multiplied in recent months. Many young people maintaining their own domiciles and experiencing acute difficulty in living on their present incomes are going in and mortgaging their furniture and their cars, if they have cars, in order to borrow from small loan companies and get by what they think is a temporary condition, but which I am afraid is going to be anything but temporary. As a consequence I fear that many of these families are going to be completely destroyed economically. That is all I intend to say on this matter at the moment, but I would suggest to the minister that this aspect of the situation be checked rather carefully.
I mentioned earlier that I desired to refer to the question of coal. I do so because, as I elso raid, the coal mining industry in Canada is suffering great stress and strain today and if appropriate action is not taken without delay the situation is likely to become far more acute. I come from a province in which is found approximately 92 per cent of Canada's coal reserves, and I represent a constituency in which coal mining is an important industry. Speaking in the house yesterday, the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) expressed certain of his

fears, and I can sympathize with the way he feels. He referred to the export of gas from Alberta to central Canada and the detrimental effect he thought that might have upon the coal mining industry and the general industrial development of the maritimes. The hon. member also registered opposition to the development of the St. Lawrence seaway project, for very similar reasons.
I am not referring to these measures for the purpose of criticizing what the hon. member had to say. I believe he is quite right to feel as he does, but I cannot agree that we should give up any idea of exporting gas and oil to central Canada, nor can I agree that we should permit the St. Lawrence project to remain undeveloped. In my opinion these things need not have a detrimental effect upon industry either in the maritimes or anywhere else, but certainly steps will have to be taken in order to obviate what could occur if we just continue to drift. As I say, I come from Alberta, where we have had tremendous gas and oil developments particularly since 1947; yet in that same province we have a tremendous coal mining industry. When I tell you that we have 92 per cent of Canada's coal reserves there; then when I tell you that last year we produced 27,595,702 barrels of crude oil; when I tell you there are 2,088 producing oil wells in Alberta-775 being at Redwater, 548 at Leduc, 329 at Turner valley and 446 in other areas; when I tell you there are 401 gas wells producing; when I tell you there were 59 million acres of crown and privately-owned land under exploration in 1950; when I tell you there were 127 drilling rigs in operation last year and that in 1950 alone they drilled over 820 miles of wells: then you will realize why the coal miner in my province is a bit exercised about what could conceivably happen to him.
I do not hold the fears some people seem to have. In the first place, as I say, I cannot believe that we should even think of retarding progress. I pm not unmindful of the fact that when the generation of electric energy was undertaken in volume a great many people felt that it would result in the destruction of not only the coal mining industry but other industries within the country. I am particularly pleased that we have had this gas and oil development. As a matter of fact, even though there are coal mines in my own constituency I do not hesitate to assert that I have joined with others in pressing to have gas brought into my town. I know that it is cheaper than coal; I know it is cleaner to handle; and I know it is easier to handle and regulate in connection with the heating of my house. At
The Budget-Mr. Shaw the same time, I must say that we in Canada must concentrate upon the development of new markets for Canadian coal. There are parts of Canada which could not conceivably be supplied with gas. We must determine new uses for coal-as a matter of fact, the word "determine" is not a good one. We already know uses to which coal can be put. We must undertake the extraction of the products that can be derived from coal when it is broken, down. Moreover, if there should be a decline in employment in the coal mining industry as a consequence of the development of gas and oil, then certainly every opportunity must be provided to enable the coal miners to become established in other fields of employment.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to mention a few more things about coal. In Alberta there is an estimated 100 billion tons, and yet in 1950 there was actually less coal mined than in 1949. I know that the big Brazeau collieries at Nordegg in my own riding were inoperative last year owing to a tragic fire which destroyed their surface workings, and that contributed to the decrease in production. Two or three other factors contributed to it as well. During that same period, however, we imported more coal from the United States into central Canada than ever before. I have heard arguments about United States coal being cheaper. I have heard arguments about its being cleaner. But if we require this product some time during a period of national stress, and! imports are cut off, cheapness and cleanliness', will not be of much consequence.
Last year there was a decrease of almost' half a million tons in coal production in the province of Alberta. Actually, four mines in the Drumheller valley were closed. There is a bright spot, though, because in January of this year coal production was 807,456 tons as compared with 761,157 tons last year. We have had government subventions paid on the delivery of western coal. There has been a maximum rate of $8.40 a ton, with a subsidy of $2.50 a ton. It was only recently that we encountered a further increase in freight rates on coal from western to central Canada. There was an increase of $2.35 per ton. We are told that at this time next year the same thing is going to happen. Mr. Speaker, it has been estimated by reliable authorities that by next year, because of our inability to find other markets, -because of our failure to take proper action in connection with freight rates, because of the development of gas and oil, the production of coal in Alberta is likely to be two million tons less than in 1950.
This would mean two things. Many mines will go out of business, and it is proper for us

The Budget-Mr. Shaw to realize at this time that you just cannot allow coal mines to go out of business, then expect to have them start up again overnight. Every time a coal mine closes, it could well be a permanent loss so far as the industry is concerned. There are 10,000 miners in my province, and 75,000 people dependent upon the industry. It is a fight for survival. The loss of the two million tons to which I referred a moment ago is computed as being the margin of profitable operation. If we do not expand our markets, and production should fall by two million tons, it is conceivable there will be a collapse of that industry in that part of Canada. As Canadians, we cannot afford to allow the coal mining industry to be smashed. This is especially true when we are in the shadow of war, and may be in the shadow of war for a long time. It is equally true when we consider the vulnerability of our oil and gas fields, as well as the vulnerability of the refineries and pipe lines.
At the moment there is an acute shortage of power in the country. Surely, there is a market for a tremendous amount of coal, -even low grade coal, if we expand our power developing industry in this country. The United States has been concentrating upon this for some time. They claim that they produce electrical energy more cheaply this way than by any other. Mr. Speaker, it all resolves itself into one very important factor. In referring to that important factor, I might well quote what the premier of Alberta recently had to say about this subject:
The production of coal in 1950 amounted to D, 118,206 tons, valued at $41,631,579 as compared with [DOT]8,616,981 tons, valued at $44,541,538 in 1949. This decline is at least partially due to the stiff competition which the coal industry is facing from oil and natural gas. The principal consumers of Alberta's bituminous coal are the two transcontinental railways and their program of conversion to oil burning and diesel locomotives makes it imperative that other markets for bituminous coal be developed.
The railways have announced that on March 31, 1951, the special freight rate of $8.40 per ton on Alberta coal moving to the Ontario market will be cancelled. The so-called normal tariff is $13.10 a ton and the railways propose to re-establish such rate by means of two increases-one of $2.35 per ton effective March 31, 1951, and a second similar increase effective a year hence. This will render substantially more difficult present efforts to establish an eastern Canadian market for Alberta coal and emphasizes the need for a national fuel policy designed to open Canadian markets to Canadian producers.
What I was coming to, Mr. Speaker, is that Canada requires a national fuel policy. May I call it six o'clock?
At six o'clock the house took recess.

maintopic: CANADIAN LEGION OF THE BRITISH EMPIRE SERVICE LEAGUE
CANADIAN LEGION OF THE BRITISH EMPIRE SERVICE LEAGUE
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 190, respecting the Canadian Legion of the British Empire Service League.

maintopic: CANADIAN LEGION OF THE BRITISH EMPIRE SERVICE LEAGUE
speechtext: Is the hon. member going to explain the bill?

maintopic: CANADIAN LEGION OF THE BRITISH EMPIRE SERVICE LEAGUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill is presented on behalf of the Canadian Legion of the British Empire Service League. I am not going to say very much about the organization, which is very well known in this country. It is a very important and a very influential organization of war veterans which reaches into every home in this Dominion of Canada.
It is a very simple bill. Its purpose is to make three changes in the act. When these changes are made the objective will have been attained, which is further to democratize the Legion. At the present time the bylaws and regulations of the Legion can be amended by the dominion executive. When the bill came before the house in 1948 some members were critical in a kindly way of that particular aspect of the bill. This bill will no longer empower the dominion executive to pass bylaws and regulations, but rather will leave it in the hands of the dominion convention.
In addition to that, it proposes to give the provincial conventions the right to enact bylaws and rules governing their own command, provided that those bylaws and rules are not inconsistent with nor contrary to any passed by the dominion convention.
Its third purpose is designed to protect the badges, insignia, and regalia against use by

persons other than those authorized by the Legion. This house will appreciate that no outsider should be permitted to capitalize on the goodwill and the reputation which the Legion bears in this country. That is all there is to the bill. I trust that it will appeal to members of the house and that we shall be able to pass it tonight.

maintopic: CANADIAN LEGION OF THE BRITISH EMPIRE SERVICE LEAGUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it
is not my intention to oppose this bill in any way. I think it will meet with general acceptance so far as the house is concerned. It is a bill which has been before the other chamber, and I understand that it was recommended by the committee of the other chamber without any amendment.
The hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) has said that the original bill as now being amended was before this house in 1948. At that time there was considerable debate on the different sections of the bill. I think that this bill corrects some of the matters which it was felt at that time should be corrected.
I should like to say a few words, Mr. Speaker, with reference to the Legion and its organization. Before 1948 I understand the Legion was organized under the different provincial companies acts, and we are not surprised that an organization of its size and extent should look for a dominion charter.
The Legion has had tremendous growth. As we all know, it started after the first world war, and then of course after the second world war it practically doubled its members. I understand that there are over 2,000 branches in Canada today, and I believe it has a membership of around 400,000. Its members consist of ex-soldiers who fought in the South African war, in the first world war and in the second world war. Now we have men who are fighting in Korea who will also be eligible for membership in the Canadian Legion. Therefore we can realize what a large place the Legion has in the life of this Dominion of Canada.
I think that the success of the Legion since its inception has been due mostly to the calibre of the men who have been directing its destinies. One has only to mention such men as General Turner, General Currie, General Crerar, General LaFleche, Brigadier General Ross, General Price, Alexander Walker and men such as those, and last but not least, our present president, Alfred Watts. These men have been outstanding not only in the Canadian Legion but in other walks of life in this country of ours.
I should like to pay tribute, if I may, to some of the secretaries of the Canadian
The Canadian Legion
Legion. As I remember, when I first came to Ottawa-and I am sure that other hon. members who attended the different veterans committees will remember-Mr. Reg. Bowler was untiring in his efforts for the advancement of returned soldiers at that time. We had the late John Herwig, who also used to appear before our veterans committees. I should like to pay a special tribute, Mr. Speaker, to a gentleman who passed away here just last month. I refer to the late Richard Hale. He was known as Dick Hale. I remember Richard Hale attending all the meetings of the veterans committees of this house since 1935, and he was attending meetings before that. Dick Hale, as we knew him, was on the staff of The Legionary for ten years. He wrote the page called "The helping hand". For thirty-three years he worked for the disabled veteran. I do not think there was anyone belonging to the Legion or outside of it, Mr. Speaker, who had a better knowledge of the Pension Act or the other acts which refer to the soldiers' welfare than had Richard Hale. A recent article in The Legionary said that he had handled over 20,000 individual claims for different returned men; therefore thousands of men have reason to be very thankful indeed to the late Richard Hale.
I should also like to say that in my opinion, Mr. Speaker, never in the history of this country have we had such a splendid organization as the Canadian Legion is. The Legion, as we know, stands for practically all that is best in this country. They have worked and are working untiringly for the betterment not only of returned men but of our country in general. At this time, when it is necessary to consider pensions, and matters connected with the cost of living, the hospitalization of veterans, as well as the question of manpower and of civil defence, we know that all these matters are receiving very careful attention from the Canadian Legion.
I am also very pleased indeed that such a powerful body as the Legion is nonpolitical, and I hope this is something the Legionnaires and the organization generally will guard jealously.
The hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) mentioned that it was an exclusive organization. As I said a moment ago, only those men who served in the South African war, or in the first or second world wars, are eligible for membership. Members of the Legion are proud indeed to belong to that organization and to wear its insignia. I am sure it is for this reason that in the bill there
2118	HOUSE OF
The Canadian Legion
is a section which will guard even more carefully the insignia of the Canadian Legion.
It is not my intention to say anything further. I am satisfied that the bill, coming as it does from the Legion, will meet with the approval of the house. So far as I am concerned, I am very pleased indeed to give it my approval.

maintopic: CANADIAN LEGION OF THE BRITISH EMPIRE SERVICE LEAGUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to join with previous speakers in paying my respects to the Canadian Legion, and its work in Canada. It is not often one has the opportunity to speak in the house about this organization, because it very rarely comes to the house with any request beyond those affecting pensions, or other matters handled through committees of the house.
I consider the Canadian Legion one of the greatest stabilizing influences in the Canadian economy and way of life. As a non-political organization, and working as it does through its committees in every town and village in the dominion, people perhaps are not fully aware of its work in those communities.
I should like to pay tribute not only to the secretaries in those branches but to the executive committees, men who not only give their time night after night to looking after the welfare of their fellow returned soldiers, but take an interest in the welfare of the whole community.
The bill aims to make the Legion still more democratic in its operation. In my view it is an advance to have dominion conventions make changes. I was wondering however if in the new section 15 there is not some weakness. We see that it says that no person except the Legion, or a person authorized in writing by the Legion, shall do certain things. My suggestion is that the meaning of the word "Legion" should be defined. Is it the provincial command, the dominion command, an individual club or a group that may be operating as a Legion in some small town?
I believe if the term is defined we will be further ahead than we are at the present time, because we know that certain local clubs have initiated drives-and I shall not mention the kind-which have not met with the approval of the command itself. As the act now reads, with the full blessing of the law a branch could carry out what is distasteful to other branches, or to the Canadian Legion command. I would ask the sponsor of the bill if he has thought of broadening the definition so as to clarify this situation. I am satisfied it is the wish of the Legion to keep the same control over its operations, and to prevent individuals or small groups from exploiting the good name and the insignia of the organization.


I am one hundred per cent behind the idea involved in the bill, and before closing my remarks I would ask for further clarification of that section. In the name of the people in my riding I pay the highest possible tribute to the work of the Canadian Legion in that part of Canada, where it has been operating for the last twenty-five years, since its inception.

maintopic: CANADIAN LEGION OF THE BRITISH EMPIRE SERVICE LEAGUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to join with other hon. members in praising the very good work of the Canadian Legion. They are a great stabilizing force in times of peace and war, and they provide an agency to which any veteran may take his grievance, in the full knowledge that the Legion will do everything within its power to see that such grievances are redressed.
I recall that when the bill to incorporate the Canadian Legion was before the house in May of 1948 several members objected to section 5 on the ground that it provided1 for an undemocratic procedure in that the executive council would have the right to repeal bylaws or rules when the dominion convention is not in session.
At that time I did not oppose the section because I felt that, in view of the fact the Legion had asked for the enactment of the legislation and the request had come from the floor of the convention, the Legion knew best what it wanted. On the other hand I am glad this amendment is before the house, making provision that the bylaws can be repealed only by the convention instead of by the executive council. I also note the amendment provides that no person except the Legion shall have the right to manufacture, distribute or sell Canadian Legion insignia or emblems or badges. This is only right because it provides employment for veterans. I recall some years ago a most unpleasant incident in connection with poppy sales. We have always looked upon the manufacture of poppies as providing employment for veterans; yet at that time we found that a large number of poppies had been manufactured in Japan and sent to this country for sale. That certainly did not meet with the wishes of the people.
In the same way, I think it is desirable that the manufacturing of insignia should be carried out by veterans. It provides employment for disabled and blind veterans. Therefore I say the amendments in the bill merit the support of the house.

maintopic: CANADIAN LEGION OF THE BRITISH EMPIRE SERVICE LEAGUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to add a few words to those already expressed on behalf of the Canadian Legion. I well remember in the years that

followed the first great war the difficult time many of us had to bring forth some such organization as this. There were many attempts made, and different forms of veteran organizations were set up before the present Canadian Legion was brought into being. I think that today the Legion is probably the most influential organization in this nation.
As has been said by my colleague the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks), they now have some two thousand branches with a membership of something over 400,000. He stated, and I agree with him, that much of the success has been due to the capable officers who have been in charge of this great organization.
Coupled with the names that have been set forth in Hansard I should like to add that of a personal friend of mine, the immediate past president, Colonel Baxter. Colonel Baxter is a very influential citizen and a good businessman who spends most of his time flying from one part of Canada to the other in connection with his business. Despite all this, he has given a great deal of time to the welfare and advancement of the Legion during the past few years. He was asked to continue in office at the last convention, but because of his business activities he found that he could not give any further time.
Mention was made of the secretaries, excomrades Bowler and Herwig, both of whom obtained their first experience with the Legion in my province of Manitoba. Both gave splendid service in the provincial command before taking office with the dominion command. They both gave great service on behalf of their comrades.
I think this amendment is much in order. I do not agree with everything in section 4 which amends section 15 of the act and which states:
No person except the Legion, or a person authorized in writing by the Legion, shall manufacture, distribute, sell, or use any Legion insignia, regalia, emblem, badge-
I think we should have some further information from the sponsor of the bill as to whether this would apply to just the executive officers. There is no more influential organization in Canada than the Canadian Legion. It would be difficult to enumerate the contributions they have made to the federal government and to this nation. During the last great war their assistance to the government of the day and to the people of this nation was invaluable. They have a stabilizing effect on the country in peacetime as well as in wartime. The civilian
The Canadian Legion
population of the country owe a debt of gratitude to the Legion.
I want to indicate my wholehearted support of the splendid work they are doing and say that I approve of these amendments.

maintopic: CANADIAN LEGION OF THE BRITISH EMPIRE SERVICE LEAGUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, any organization with the fine reputation gained by the Canadian Legion during world war I, after world war I and during world war II should receive the consideration they are asking for with this bill. As one who had the honour of serving in the Royal Canadian Naval Volunteer Reserve I think I should say on behalf of the naval veterans that they have received great consideration and help from the Canadian Legion. In the part of the country from which I come there are five branches of the Canadian Legion. As the previous speaker has said, they have done great work in peacetime as well as during wartime and this bill commends itself to me as I think it will to other hon. members.
With regard to the amendment to section 15, I suppose there are those who take advantage of the insignia, emblems and other articles that might be sold by the Canadian Legion, so it is proper that they should be given the right to stipulate who shall have authority to sell these articles. Mention has been made of possible confusion with regard to the Legion. I have not the act before me but I would imagine the phraseology would be interpreted in the interpretation section of the act.

maintopic: CANADIAN LEGION OF THE BRITISH EMPIRE SERVICE LEAGUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to join with other hon. members in paying tribute to the Canadian Legion. There are a number of Legion branches in my riding and I say without qualification that they are exceedingly well managed and contribute a great deal to the well-being of the veterans and their families and to the general welfare of the whole district. The Legion branches have sponsored many worth-while activities-to mention only a few: community centre projects, hospital drives, the founding of high school and collegiate scholarships and so on, We have learned in Grey North that when a worthy cause is before the public the members of the Legion are solidly behind it. The Legion is playing an important part in the furtherance of Canadian citizenship.
In the old days the Legion was an army organization. Being interested particularly in the R.C.A.F., I am glad to say that the Legion today is a harmonious amalgamation of members of the three services. As would be expected, the president of the Legion is a former air force officer, Group Captain A.

The Canadian Legion
Watts, A.F.C., a world war II pilot and an efficient administrator. Group Captain Watts and the dominion executive council are providing aggressive and able leadership for the Canadian Legion organization.
As previous speakers have said, there is nothing particularly contentious about this bill. The first two amendments are constitutional changes requested by the Legion while the third amendment aims to protect the insignia, regalia and badges of the Canadian Legion. This is a very necessary amendment. As has been stated, the general public will be protected by this amendment because these articles will have to have the approval of the Secretary of State (Mr. Bradley). I am sure that this bill commends itself to the house.

maintopic: CANADIAN LEGION OF THE BRITISH EMPIRE SERVICE LEAGUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to commend this bill to the members of the house. As has been said more eloquently than I could say it by other hon. members who have spoken, the Canadian Legion is worthy of our support. I have a slightly different background from that of many of those who have spoken. I was denied the opportunity of enlisting in two world wars. Like a great many others in a similar position, I have a sort of complex with respect to matters of this kind.
When the nation is in danger and uniforms are worn by so many one feels that perhaps he is not doing his full share in the national interest. I have had that feeling keenly from time to time, as I suppose many others have, but there is not much one could do about it. Because of that background I welcome the chance to support the Canadian Legion on an occasion such as this when they come before us asking for amendments to their charter.
I think perhaps the proudest night in my life was about two years ago when the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg), then Minister of Veterans Affairs, came to our branch of the Canadian Legion of the British Empire Service League in Brampton on which occasion I was given an honorary membership in the organization. I look back on that night with the greatest of pride.
During the period between the two great wars and during the last war and since there has been a well-founded feeling that the Legion is in the forefront of all things that are worth while and worthy of patriotic Canadianism. Those feelings have found their core and centre in the Canadian Legion of the British Empire Service League.
We appreciate the opportunity of saying a word on behalf of an organization that has meant so much to Canada, to the empire-

yes, and to the world. I can speak tonight with perhaps a little more feeling and emotion than usual in supporting a bill like this which is designed to help the people who have made it possible for us to sit in this chamber and to legislate instead of having a different system of government under which we might be living today were it not for their valiant efforts. It is easy to forget over the years because time changes things so much. It is so easy for us to forget that between wars, as was the case between the last two world wars, there must be someone like the Legion, prepared to carry the torch of patriotism, endeavour and activity in the interest of all that is best in our national life. All these things the Legion has done and will continue to do. I might say again that one of the proudest moments of my life was when I was admitted as one of the members of that great band of men and women who have left and are leaving their mark for better citizenship and for the advancement and the betterment of Canada as a whole.

maintopic: CANADIAN LEGION OF THE BRITISH EMPIRE SERVICE LEAGUE
speechtext: In Brampton they always say it with flowers, and wonderfully too.

maintopic: CANADIAN LEGION OF THE BRITISH EMPIRE SERVICE LEAGUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as another member of the Legion I want to join wholeheartedly in supporting this bill. I want to join with other members from all sides of the house in the nice things that have been said and the tributes that have been paid to the Canadian Legion. The many compliments that have been paid to the Legion are well deserved because the Legion has done a wonderful job. I do not think that any other party or club should be allowed to use the insignia or any other emblem or regalia that the Canadian Legion have used over the last twenty-five years. I do not want to take up the time of the house.
I merely want to say that I wholeheartedly support the bill.

maintopic: CANADIAN LEGION OF THE BRITISH EMPIRE SERVICE LEAGUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too should like to associate myself with those who have spoken. I consider that the members of the Canadian Legion are the first citizens of Canada. I think we owe more to them than to any other group in our population. Therefore they are deserving of every consideration. It is not often we have a bill before the house on which all members on both sides can agree.
